[...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. It is a high-performance insulating film used inside the packaging substrate that sits between a chip and a circuit board. Simply put, it is the green plastic-y bit under the metal bit of a processor. Without it, high-frequency signals would cross-contaminate, and even the most advanced processor would fail. [...] Ajinomoto discovered ABF as a byproduct of amino acid chemistry in the 1970s, collaborated with Intel in 1996 to develop it into a practical product, and began mass production in 1999. Today, it commands over 95% of the global market for ABF materials used in CPU and GPU packaging. Its only competitor, Sekisui Chemical, holds roughly 5%. [...] ABF is the most dramatic example. Every processor, GPU, FPGA, and AI accelerator needs a chip carrier. It’s a substrate that bridges the chip to the circuit board, and almost all of them use ABF as the insulating layer. Modern desktop processors contain up to 2,000 copper traces running through their carrier; server-grade AI chips have many times more. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. snippet: What makes the current copper setup so interesting is not that the market is wrong, but that it is incomplete in a very specific way. Most participants already understand that demand is going higher, and in fact, that part of the thesis has become consensus. You hear the same numbers repeated across desks: roughly 25 million tonnes of annual demand today, moving toward 35–40 million tonnes over the next decade, driven by electrification, AI infrastructure, renewable energy, and increasingly electrified defense systems. There is no edge in restating those drivers. The edge sits in recognizing that these forecasts assume a system that behaves more smoothly than the real one does. Because copper does not exist as a number — it exists as a chain of physical processes, and those processes do not scale linearly. They stretch, they delay, and eventually, they bottleneck. [...] The easiest way to see this is to stop thinking about copper as supply and start thinking about copper as movement. Production data alone gives a misleading sense of stability. The United States produces just over 1.1 million tonnes annually, Canada contributes roughly 0.5 million tonnes, and at first glance, that suggests a region with meaningful supply capacity. But once you follow the material, the structure looks very different. In 2023, the U.S. still imported approximately 890,000 tonnes of refined copper, while Canada exported around 450,000 tonnes of concentrate, most of it to Asia for processing. This means the system is not self-contained; it is dependent on long-distance logistics and external refining capacity. Copper is mined in one place, processed in another, and consumed in a third. The current shock raises the specter of spillovers to the U.S. through both prices and physical shortages of goods. Those custom tags, which are not comparable across companies, are filtered out of this view by design. [...] Revenue is always`USD` for US filers. snippet: The conflict in the Middle East has precipitated a global supply shock—the third in six years following the pandemic in 2020 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The current shock raises the specter of spillovers to the U.S. through both prices and physical shortages of goods. A critical conduit for spillovers through these channels is via Asian supply chains, especially from middle- to lower-middle income countries in southeast Asia, which are key suppliers for goods needed for the AI infrastructure build-out in the U.S. These countries are also heavily reliant on Middle East energy imports. This post examines key factors related to these Asian supply chain vulnerabilities. [...] fifth of global [...] chart below of [...] New York Fed [...] GSCPI [...] The GSCPI extracts the supply signal from survey data on manufacturing industry delivery times, order backlogs, and inventory stocks as well as shipping costs for ocean and airfreight.
